analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Medicaid cuts and work requirements in the 2025 reconciliation law.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by one House Democrat with no cosponsors, sits in two House committees with no action and no vote as of the end of the record.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would undo the Medicaid provisions of the 2025 spending law known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Those provisions require many Medicaid recipients to work, volunteer, or train to keep coverage; restrict federal Medicaid payments for people who are not citizens or certain legal residents; and limit the taxes states use to help fund Medicaid. The bill would restore the rules as if those provisions had never passed. It was referred to two House committees and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, low-income adults on Medicaid — including the expansion population who would face work requirements — would keep coverage they could otherwise lose, and lawfully residing immigrant families would keep or regain access to Medicaid and CHIP. Hospitals and state budgets would also benefit from fewer uninsured patients and restored state financing flexibility.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the chapter of Public Law 119-21 that added work and community-engagement requirements for the Medicaid expansion population, restoring coverage rules as if that chapter had never been enacted [S2][S3].

Would reverse the restriction, starting in fiscal year 2027, on federal Medicaid and CHIP payment for services to people who are not U.S. citizens, lawful permanent residents, or specified legally residing categories such as Cuban-Haitian entrants and Compact of Free Association migrants [S2].
Would undo the limits on state Medicaid provider taxes beginning in fiscal year 2027, a financing tool many states use to draw federal matching funds [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The federal government would bear the cost of the Medicaid spending the 2025 law cut, and opponents of the original cuts' goals would point to higher federal Medicaid outlays; no group in the bill text bears a new direct cost.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the provisions restores federal Medicaid spending that the 2025 law had reduced, adding to federal outlays; the repeal bill itself contains no offsetting savings [S2][S3].
Supporters of the underlying law argue the work requirements and eligibility limits reduce spending and target benefits; this bill rejects those policies wholesale rather than modifying them [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a straightforward repeal with no negotiation: it restores prior Medicaid rules but adds nothing new and pays for the restored spending with higher federal deficits. The main cost is federal; the main benefit is coverage kept by people who would otherwise face work requirements or eligibility screens.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees, and nothing further has happened to it.

narrative.text: Rep. Brendan Boyle introduced the bill on June 30, 2026, and it was referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and, in addition, the Committee on Ways and Means [S1][S5].
No committee action, floor action, or vote appears in the record after the referral, and the bill has no cosponsors [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one yet — the Medicaid provisions the bill targets remain in place, and the bill has not advanced far enough for anyone to have won or lost because of it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; bill is pending

sides.party_line_note: The bill has a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party; the House majority is Republican, and the law it would amend passed with Republican support in 2025.

industries.note: Repealing the Medicaid provisions would keep or restore coverage for patients, reducing uncompensated care and protecting revenue, especially for hospitals serving low-income and rural communities. The bill's outcome so far leaves the cuts in place.
The bill would undo limits on Medicaid provider taxes beginning in FY2027, giving states back a financing tool used to draw federal matching funds.
Coverage losses from the 2025 law's work requirements and eligibility restrictions shrink Medicaid managed-care enrollment; repeal would preserve that enrollment.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and referral to two committees controlled by the majority party, the bill is very unlikely to get a markup or floor vote this Congress; bills like this typically die in committee when the session ends in January 2027.
